definition: In the field of artificial intelligence (AI), tasks that are hypothesized to require artificial general intelligence to solve are informally known as AI-complete or AI-hard.
details: Calling a problem AI-complete reflects the belief that it cannot be solved by a simple specific algorithm. Prior to 2013, problems supposed to be AI-complete included computer vision, natural language understanding, and dealing with unexpected circumstances while solving any real-world problem. AI-complete tasks were notably considered useful for distinguishing humans from automated agents, as CAPTCHAs aim to do.

explainer.lead: AI-complete is an informal label for problems thought to require artificial general intelligence, rather than a narrowly designed algorithm. It captures the difficulty of tasks such as understanding language, interpreting visual scenes, and adapting to unexpected situations in the real world.

tiers.eli5: Some jobs are easy to give a computer exact instructions for, but others seem to require the flexible understanding people use every day. People call those especially broad jobs AI-complete. It is like knowing how to get around an unfamiliar place when something surprising happens: following one fixed set of directions is not enough.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers encounter the idea when scoping open-ended problems in vision, language, and autonomous systems. Restricted versions can be built with expert systems or modern models, but success on a narrow task does not establish robust handling of unexpected real-world circumstances. Machine translation is now among the capabilities of large language models, illustrating how practical progress can occur without resolving the full generality implied by the label.
tiers.paperLevel: Yampolskiy defines a problem C as AI-Complete if C is Human Oracle-solvable and every AI problem can be converted into C by a polynomial-time algorithm. A problem H is AI-Hard if and only if some AI-Complete problem C is polynomial-time Turing-reducible to H. Because many AI problems have not been formally characterized, conventional computational complexity theory does not supply a general formal definition of AI-completeness; Šekrst also argues that a polynomial solution would not necessarily settle artificial general intelligence.

explainer.example: Consider autonomous driving beyond a controlled setting. A system may recognize objects in ordinary cases, yet still need to understand the general context and adjust when an unexpected situation arises; if handling that full range of real-world circumstances requires general intelligence, the problem fits the intended AI-complete label.

usedIn.name: CAPTCHAs
usedIn.detail: Tasks considered AI-complete were seen as useful for distinguishing people from automated agents, which is the goal of CAPTCHAs.

usedIn.name: Expert systems
usedIn.detail: Systems popular in the 1980s solved simple or restricted versions of these problems, but became brittle when scaled to unfamiliar situations.

usedIn.name: Large language models
usedIn.detail: Capabilities such as machine translation cover tasks once considered AI-complete, without making the informal label a formal complexity result.

usedIn.name: Gato
usedIn.detail: DeepMind's 2022 model combined activities including Atari play, image captioning, chatting, and robot-arm block stacking in one model.

explainer.intuition: The label marks problems for which a simple, specific algorithm is believed to be insufficient. Its core intuition is that broad contextual understanding and adaptability—not just performance on a fixed, narrow version—are needed.
howItWorks: Start with an open-ended AI task, such as natural language understanding.
Ask whether solving it in full generality would require artificial general intelligence.
If so, describe it informally as AI-complete or AI-hard.
Distinguish restricted implementations from a solution that handles unexpected real-world circumstances.
explainer.whyItMatters: AI-completeness separates narrow task performance from the broader adaptability associated with general intelligence. It also explains why early expert systems could succeed in restricted settings yet fail when situations moved outside their original problem context.
misconceptions: AI-complete is not simply another name for NP-complete: the term was coined by analogy, but many AI problems lack the formalization needed for a conventional complexity definition.
Solving a restricted version or benchmark does not necessarily solve the problem in full generality.
Strong performance by a modern model on a formerly AI-complete task does not by itself demonstrate artificial general intelligence.
